utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution had a preliminary matter to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours and good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just a small matters and it relates to the testimony of Branko Basara, and a document that we intend to use with Mr. Basara. On Friday, the Prosecution sent an e-mail regarding a revised translation of a document that will be used with Basara. The document in question is P2365 and the Prosecution advised that it had uploaded a revised draft of that -- a revised translation of that document and the doc ID 00478672-ET and the Prosecution requests that the Court Officer be instructed to replace the existing translation with the revised translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the Defence looked at the new translation? Is it just minor details or is it more. I mean, does it have any affect on previous witness through which the document was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It doesn't have an affect on the previous witness so far as I understand it. There are some changes to the translation to the previous draft translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. But of minor importance but precision. Has the Defence had a look at the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I just saw it printed on the table. I didn't even pick it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that we instruct the Registrar to replace the present English translation by the new one and that you have a possibility to revisit the matter, well, let's say within the next -- when is the witness scheduled to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Today, yes. Then have a look at it as quickly as possible and if the -- have the changes been notified? Does the Defence know where the changes are in the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I can certainly sit with Mr. Lukic in the next break and draw his attention to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be good so you can work more focussed on it. Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to replace the existing English translation of P2365 by the new one, which has doc ID 00478672-ET. Before we continue, I'd like to briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Could we please call Witness Andja Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the representative of the Registry at the other side of the videolink inform the Chamber about the presence of -- who is present in the videolink room apart from you and the witness as we can see on our screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honours. Apart from the two of us, we have the IT representative from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Ms. Obradovic. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Witness. Please be seated. Witness, before we start, has the Defence explained the procedure we'll follow today, that is, that you'll be invited to attest to a statement you have earlier given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before court you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So are you aware, because most likely we'll not hear any substance of your evidence but your evidence is in a written statement and that you appear mainly to attest to the accuracy and the truthfulness of that statement. Is that clear, this procedure we'll follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Stojanovic, who is counsel for Mr. Mladic, will now put a few questions to you. Carefully listen and please answer the questions. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]Once again, good morning. Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you to speak slowly and give us your exact name and surname.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Andja Obradovic, born on the 10th of June, 1956. 1956. Titovnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, did you give a statement to the Defence of General Mladic or specifically to me as one of his Defence attorneys? Did you give a statement in writing?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, without having this broadcast, could we please take a look at the mentioned statement, namely the first page of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give Madam Registrar a number, then she'll be able to have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I can assist you, Mr. Stojanovic, it seems to be 1D1661.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. 1D1661.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I hope, Madam, that now you see the statement before you, and this is what I'm asking you: Can you recognise the signature on this first page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to ask that we look at the last page of this document, which is 65 ter 1D1661. Madam, the signature that you see on this page, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the date that is written there, the 7th of August, 2014, is that also written in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I'd like to ask you: Today, now that you've taken this oath before this Court stating that you will tell the truth, would you fully stand by what was written in this statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And would this statement represent your entire knowledge and experience concerning the events that you testified about?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to read a brief summary of this witness's statement, and I would kindly ask that this be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the purpose of reading a summary is to inform the public. So, therefore, if the statement will be confidential, then it may make no much sense to -- to give the summary because the Judges have read the statement. And I take it you want to tender --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Then out of an abundance of caution for the reasons that we already mentioned we would not read this summary, but this is a good opportunity for me to tender this witness's statement into evidence in this case under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we decide on that -- Witness, did you have an opportunity to review your statement recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's on that basis that you attested to the accuracy and the truthfulness of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CORLISS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1661 receives number D1029.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence, under seal. Witness, your appearance in court was very short. That doesn't mean that your testimony is not important but we have read your statement and that's what we'll consider. Therefore, even though being short -- being in court only for a very short period of time, I would like to thank you very much for appearing, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution earlier has indicated that there are no questions for this witness. That's the reason why no further questions will be put to you. I would, nevertheless, thank you very much for coming to the videolink location, for having attested to your statement which is now in evidence. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the witness can be escorted out of the videolink room.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the next witness which was scheduled we do understand that he is unable to appear today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, my next question is: Would the witness scheduled after that witness, is the Defence ready to call that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we are calling Mr. Vasiljevic, Borislav.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Who would also testified by videolink and for whom the Prosecution has also indicated there are no further questions apart from attestation that there is no need to cross-examine that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CORLISS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that the witness, the next witness has appeared in the videolink room. Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic. Could you please stand. Before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth and from the fact that you are standing, I take it that can you hear me -- you can see me and hear me in a language you understand? I heard a soft "da," perhaps too soft for our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The solemn declaration -- the text of the solemn declaration will now be handed out to you, and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. Please be seated. Mr. Vasiljevic, has the procedure which we'll follow today, been explained to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that only questions will be put for the purpose of an attestation of the statement you've given earlier and that you'll not be cross-examined on it. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to start your examination-in-chief, which will be very short, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Vasiljevic, you'll now be examined by Mr. Lukic. He'll put a few questions to you. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please slowly state your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Borislav Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the screen now could we please have 1D01740. Mr. Vasiljevic, do you see this on the screen or do you have a hard copy of your statement before you, on paper?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I have a statement before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So have you opened the first page? I mean, the very first page. And do you see a signature on it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose is it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Mine, mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you please be so kind as to take a look at the last page of your statement. Can you see a signature on this document and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I do recognise it. It is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The statement before you, did you provide it to the members of the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the statement accurately reflect what you told the Defence team members on behalf of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The contents of the statement, have they been recorded to the best of your recollection and accuracy?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is 100 per cent accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. At this point in time, we seek to tender Mr. Vasiljevic's statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, can we just confirm that the date mentioned in paragraph 6 is correct on the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Says he returned to his parents' place on 13th of July, 2013. The same statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm, mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, can we go to paragraph 6 of your statement, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It is in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, we find the following. The reason for my return to Vasiljevici village was to make my wife and my child, who was less than two years old, to Slovenia since the war in BiH had already started. The next sentence is: "I returned to my parents' place on the 13th of July, 2013 and as early as the next day, the village was attacked by the Muslim forces from Vecici. The attack started at dawn." I apologise to you as well as to the Chamber. This detail seems to have slipped my attention. Kindly tell us whether the date as recorded is accurate, especially in terms of the year. What should be the year?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: 1992. That is when I returned from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. And thank you, Judge Moloto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that it's only the year that is wrong but that the date, the 13th of July, is accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I don't recall the date exactly. I can't be 100 per cent sure, but I think it is the correct date and the year was definitely 1992. It was a long time ago and I don't recall the precise date, but I do think it is the 13th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. No objections to the admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CORLISS
utterances.text: No objections with that corrected date, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1740 receives number D1030.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will, at this moment just read the short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness does not necessarily have to remain in the videolink room for that purposes. So if the witness would prefer to leave already he is free to do so. Mr. Vasiljevic, a short summary of your evidence will be read. Do you want to remain in the videolink room or would you already prefer to be excused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Lukic will now read a short summary of your statement. Please be aware that it's not the summary that is in evidence but it's your statement. It is just to inform the public about the content of your statement. So there's no need to make any corrections or to add anything to what Mr. Lukic will now read. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Borislav Vasiljevic testifies about the events in the municipality of Kotor Varos in early 1992. When he heard that an armed incident happened in Kotor Varos on 11th June 1992, he returned home from Slovenia where he was temporarily employed. He returned with the aim of taking care of his family. He was not mobilised and had a civilian status. He states that in late June 1992, the Muslim forces from Vecici village attacked village Staza and hamlet Vasilijevici. Jugoslav Mirjanic was killed in the attack and several villagers were wounded. His village was attacked again on 13 July 1992. He and his father were captured and taken to Vecici where they were tortured. During his captivity in Vecici, he talks in detail about the torture. He indicates names of the people who inflicted torture. He also tells names of the people who were captured, brought in, taken away, tortured and killed. Mr. Vasiljevic talks about the historical context of the suffering of the Serbs in Kotor Varos and their fear that the crimes from the Second World War might repeat. That was the short summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Vasiljevic, no further questions will be put to you. That doesn't mean that your testimony is not important for us but we received it in writing and we'll consider it with all the other evidence this Chamber receives. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to the videolink location, and I wish you a --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, we have some difficulty with the audio. We are unable to hear you from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it can be resolved quickly or whether it would take more time. Could I ask the representative of the Registry at the other side of the videolink whether he can hear me in the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I can hear you now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, would you please pass on to the witness our thanks for having come to the videolink location and convey to him that we wish him a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what language you will do that, but that's -- is there any way you can pass on that message?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looks as if at least the video is functioning again. I'm not certain about the audio. Could the representative of the Registry tell us whether the audio in both languages on the other side of the videolink is functioning well?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, English channel is functioning fine. The B/C/S channel is just being checked and I'm told it's okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we can continue. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour. We are calling Mr. Branko Basara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the videolink room. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, just while the witness is being escorted in, just to draw to the Chamber's attention the fact that there is an indictment has been issued by the Bosnian State Court against this witness in 2014 and that indictment implicates a number of scheduled incidents in the indictment before this Chamber and therefore the Prosecution considers it appropriate to advise the witness of his rights under Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the incident in the indictment against the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- may I invite you to make that, to read the text and pronounce the words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Basara. Please be seated. Mr. Basara, before I invite the Defence to examine you I'd like to inform you about the content of Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, and I'll read it to you. It reads: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Mr. Basara, this means that you can address me if you think that a truthful answer to one of the questions might incriminate yourself. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Basara, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Basara.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind to tell us your first and last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: My name is Branko Basara. I was born on the 3rd of October, 1939 in the village of Otis in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Basara, did you at some point provide a statement to the members of General Mladic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I did provide a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D1720 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You do have the written statement in front of you, Mr. Basara, do you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the front -- the cover page of the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see a signature there and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the last page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see a signature there and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I do see it. It is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The contents of the statement, have they been recorded accurately in terms of what you told the members of General Mladic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes, it was recorded correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are the contents truthful to the best of your recollection in terms of those past events?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: In terms of the contents I stated, it is all truthful in the sense of how I saw and experienced those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you answer the same way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I think I would answer them in the same way. Perhaps not word for word, but that would be the gist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we seek to tender Mr. Basara's statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1720 receives number D1031.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think the number is too big.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document receives number D1031.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1031 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, with the Court's permission, I'd like to put some additional questions to you. First of all, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there's no problem in putting additional questions to the witness but the usual practice is to read the summary first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Basara, I apologise. I skipped ahead a little too much. I was first supposed to read out the summary of your statement. I distributed to everybody but I cannot find my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd like to do it after the break, there's no problem, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That gives you time to retrieve it. Please proceed, meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then can I proceed with the questions first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Basara, did you testify previously before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I did testify - also via videolink - as a Prosecution witness concerning two people from the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes, Stanisic/Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Kindly go to paragraphs 9 and 10 in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if we can have them -- paragraph 9 on our screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the ethnic makeup in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we need the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The top of the page which is the last part of paragraph 9 where you discuss the division of the town. And about which part was to go to which part of the population. In paragraph 10, you discuss the police and the division therein. Did you play any part in those negotiations about the division or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I was present at a meeting which took place in the municipal assembly building. Not all members were present, but there were people on the Serb and the Muslim side. They were the more influential members of the assembly who discussed how to divide the town. I was present but was not involved in any decision-making. I was neutral in those talks of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you seek clarification as to members of what? It says: "Not all members were present." Members of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, you heard Judge Orie's question.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I heard the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you answer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I had in mind all members of the assembly. So the inner part of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly was present with representatives of Muslims, Serbs and Croats being in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether any agreement was reached on the division of other towns in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I know something about Bihac. I know that a division was agreed upon there as well. The right bank of the town was to be Serbian; and the left bank of the town was to be Muslim. However, the Muslims managed to take over the part that was supposed to go to the Serbs, and the Serbs were, for the most part, pushed out of Bihac. I also know something about Krupa, Bosanska Krupa. There was also an agreement there that the part of town on the right bank of the town be Serbian; the left bank, Muslim. However, the Muslims there fooled the Serbs as well, taking part the side of town that was supposed to go to the Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... reading that summary statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you found it, it's -- it's approximately time for the break. So perhaps you start with the summary after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. After the break, Mr. Lukic will first read that short summary of your statement and then he'll continue and ask further questions, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take the break first and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to check whether the videolink is still operative.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, we can hear and see you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will proceed with reading statement summary of Mr. Basara. It will be a bit longer than usually. Branko Basara was the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade in 1992. He was a retired JNA colonel until he reactivated in October 1991 to take command of the 6th Krajina Brigade. Mr. Basara always endeavoured to prevent conflicts. Through talks with Muslims, Croats and Serbs and their representatives from the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most, I tried to defuse the heated situation and some conciliatory decisions were made in this direction. Agreement was reached to divide Sanski Most into a Muslim and a Serb part. The Muslim representatives took possession of the municipal building in Sanski Most and after the Serb leadership decided to recapture the municipal building. And after that the Serb leadership decided to recapture the municipal building. Mr. Basara and his brigade is not take part in the capturing of the municipal building. Mr. Basara used to go to the Muslim villages with Nijaz Halilovic, a Muslim, convincing the inhabitants not to cause conflicts with their Serb neighbours or members of the 6th Brigade. After the withdrawal of the JNA from the Republic of Croatia, JNA was tasked with preventing interethnic conflicts. His unit implemented the task successfully until the attack of the Muslim forces on the JNA in Sarajevo, at Dobrovoljacka Street. After the attack at Dobrovoljacka Street, an order arrived to disarm the Muslim paramilitary formations. In the course of weapons confiscation his unit did not arrest those who possessed it but only took their weapons. The disarming was conducted in two stages. The first stage involved informing the Muslims and Croats in all the villages that they should voluntarily turn in all the weapons in their possession. In the second stage, the units were to go to the villages inhabited by Muslims and Croats and seize the weapons from those who had not turned them in. Armed fightings would occur where the Muslim forces offered armed resistance. Before fighting, an announcement was made that all those who did not want to fight should leave. For example, all of those who wished to exit Mahala were given a three-hour deadline to pull out. A lot of women, children and the elderly pulled out from Mahala, and even some of the able-bodied men. These people were protected by the army. According to Mr. Basara's own assessment of the situation, he decided to engage parts of the 6th Brigade in order to ensure a peaceful take-over of power in the municipality of Kljuc without conflicts and unnecessary bloodshed. Furthermore, he will testify on the nature and role of Sanski Most Crisis Staff and that he was not a member of the municipal Crisis Staff. He will further testify about the existence of paramilitaries and their relationship with the authorities and the VRS. Mr. Basara will testify that the army had nothing to do with prisons in Sanski Most, i.e., that he had no jurisdiction over those prisons and that the army did not establish prisons. Army did not play any part in the departures of the population. Mr. Basara will testify that there were a number of employed Muslims in the territory of Sanski Most who went to work regularly. He knows that there were Muslims working at the Kamengrad coal-mine. He knows this because the army was providing security for the coal-mine. And that was the short summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Basara, now I would like to continue with my questions, if you're ready.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you whether the members of the 6th Sana Brigade were deployed in the town of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Units of the 6th Brigade were not deployed in the broad area of Sanski Most. I just had one unit consisting of about 40 to 50 men near the TO storage area in Sanski Most to protect that facility in order to prevent any clashes when that facility was being taken over as well as the weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a clarification: Is the 6th Sana Brigade the same thing as the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, could you please tell us, what the exact name of your unit is.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: From the moment when this brigade was established, when I was appointed commander, it bore the name of the 6th Krajina Brigade because it inherited that brigade from the Second World War. However, later, the leadership from Pale changed its name, and they called it the Sana Brigade. So it's one and the same brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before this, you were speaking about a possible conflict involving the TO storage area or warehouse. Do you -- can you tell us what kind of information you had about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I received a lot of information about both Muslims and Serbs getting ready to take over that warehouse and the weapons that were still in that warehouse. They both wanted to get their hands on that. So ultimately I decided to move it out, and I moved it to Lusci Palanka so that it would not be a conflict involving that warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who helped you when these weapons were moved out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Nijaz Halilovic helped me the most. Up until then, he was commander of the TO Staff, and he's the one who co-operated with me the most in preventing conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nijaz Halilovic, what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: He's a Muslim, but it was my understanding that his orientation was Yugoslav, just like my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you something about the take-over of power in Sanski Most. The 6th Krajina Brigade, or, as it was later called, the 6th Sana Brigade, did it take part in the take-over of power?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I would not say take-over of power because there was a division of power. That is to say, the municipality -- well, they divided power into the Serb municipality and the Muslim municipality. However, when the police was divided, then the police and the Muslim leadership took the building of the municipality. So that was no take-over. That is to say, it was the Muslims who violently took over the municipality, the 6th brigade did not take part in that at all, and it didn't take part in any of this later either, because there weren't any units that could help either the Serbs or somebody else. On the contrary. I helped the Muslims so they could get out of the municipality when I heard who was attacking and then I made it possible for them to get out without fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us just briefly how this happened and what your role was in getting the Muslim policemen out of the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: That happened on that day when I was getting the weapons out of the storage area. And I had just completed that and went to the command post in Lusci Palanka. It may have been 9.00 p.m. Sabic would call me and asked me, Colonel, sir, do you know that an attack is it being prepared against the municipality building. I said that I had no idea whatsoever, as was indeed the case. I asked him on the basis of what and I certainly received information that they are getting ready to attack the municipality and then I suggested to him that his people should get out of the municipal building because it is not worth sacrificing a single life for some building. Then in the hotel, there were some military policemen. I called them and they helped these people get out of the building without any jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you something about the Crisis Staff. Did you attend, and do you remember how often you attended sessions of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I attended sessions of the Crisis Staff whenever I was invited and when I had the possibility to do that because I wished to be in a position to follow the situation in the area of Sanski Most on the basis of which I could make decisions of my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the work of the Crisis Staff by voting for decisions of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I never voted and I never made decisions, but I tried to exercise influence so that the decisions that they made would be as normal as possible, if you will, so that the other side would not be affected, so that the rules of warfare would be observed and everything else in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever issue any order to your units on the basis of any decision made by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: There's not a single order of mine that invokes any decisions of the Crisis Staff, and I never acted on the basis of these decisions because I did not consider them to be my superiors because I had the corps command and I only carried --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking for a repetition of the last part of the sentence -- the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, the very last part of your answer has not been recorded. I'm going to read out the last sentence in the English so that you could get the right interpretation so please just finish your thought. [In English} I quote: "A. There was not a single order of mine that invokes any decisions of the Crisis Staff, and I never acted on the basis of these decisions because I did not consider them to be my superiors because I had a corps command and I only carried --" end of quote. [Interpretation] So what did you say at the very end of your answer? Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I said that not a single order was written and in the brigade command there is no such order that invokes decisions of the Crisis Staff because I did not consider them to be my superiors. Because there was the corps command and also there was the military chain of command, and I observed that and I carried out those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know while you were in Sanski Most as commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade, did General Talic come to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: While I was commander of the brigade, General Talic did not come to Sanski Most at all, and he didn't come to the brigade command either. At one meeting -- actually, it was Lieutenant-Colonel Talic who came several times. He had been in Banja Luka. I think that his first name was Mustafa, he is a Muslim. And once he attended a session of the Crisis Staff. As for General Talic, I know for sure that he did not come at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How can you be sure that he never came?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is impossible to interpret when this is the quality of the sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please again answer that question put to you by Mr. Lukic where he asked you: How can you be sure that he - meaning General Talic - never came.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm sure because when -- if he would come to the area of Sanski Most, he would inform me, for sure, and he would come to the brigade command to see what we were doing and how we were doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to the rules of service, would have you to be notified if your commander came to the territory of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I believe that that would have been his obligation to notify me of his arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As commander of the brigade, what was your position vis-à-vis the organs of municipal government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: As for the organs of municipal government, I believed that since the municipality had power, a state of war had not been declared so they had authority over the territory of the municipality of Sanski Most. At that time I was a peace-time commander, and I did not have any right whatsoever to issue any kind of orders to the municipality organs or to interfere with their work or compel them to carry out some tasks that I would give them. Rather, through conversations, I tried to influence their work so that it would be as proper as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The municipal authorities, did they try to interfere with your work?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The municipal authorities always tried to interfere in the work of the brigade, and they tried to subordinate the brigade to them so that the brigade would be a municipal unit. However, I, as a professional, knew that I should not allow that and I did not allow that, although they tried to do that in every conceivable way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have another question to ask you about the brigade. Did your brigade have or play any part in the establishment and running of prisons which existed at the time in Sanski Most, first and foremost the Krings and Betonirka prisons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: As I said already, there was no state of war declared. I was a peacetime commander in that sense and had no right to establish camps or collection centres. In that regard, I did not take any part in such activities. I never entered any collection camp or centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did your brigade or its members take part in the transport of people to Manjaca from the Krings and Betonirka prisons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The brigade did not take any part in the transport of people to anywhere or in the process of moving people out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As the brigade commander, did you address the population on the radio or did you go to -- in the field to meet with the members of the population?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I never addressed them by radio and I contacted with the population - Muslims for the most part - with Nijaz Halilovic. We tried to speak to them against engaging the military and against causing incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with Nijaz Halilovic after the outbreak of the conflict, if you can tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: When the conflict occurred and when the Serbs regained possession of the municipal building, although I don't know precisely because I wasn't informed of it, but when they were arresting the Muslim leadership they arrested Nijaz Halilovic as well, taking him to Manjaca. I was away when it was done. I was in Belgrade to see my family since they had fled to Belgrade. Upon my return, I heard of his arrest. I was very bitter about the situation, and I promised myself to find a way to get Nijaz out. I knew he was not an extremist and that he should not have been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Did you go to Manjaca yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: First I went to see General Talic. I explained to him what Nijaz was involved in together with me and how much assistance he provided. I told him he was not a extremist and I asked him to try and come up with a solution for Nijaz's release. He did so and together with Mirko Adamovic who I think worked for the court at the time - I don't know whether he was a judge though - we went to Manjaca together. On the basis of the approval we received, we took Nijaz out of the camp, taking him to Mirko's apartment. He was there until I left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you left for Belgrade. What happened with Nijaz following your departure?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I kept Nijaz in the apartment since I did not want him to go to the territory of Sanski Most in case somebody tried to liquidate him. When I went to Belgrade, I dressed him in a uniform with a white belt to act as my escort until we crossed the border into Serbia. His father left a passport and 200 marks for him so that could further -- travel further to Austria and rejoin his family. When he crossed into Serbia, he took off the uniform, put on civilian clothes and left together with a surgeon who was accompanied by his family. They all went to Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something about mobilisation. Please tell us what the difference is between a mobilisation process in the brigade as opposed to battalion. What is the difference? What was this armed force of yours like? Can you explain to us the situation back then.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The difference was that there's mention of brigade mobilisation in different documents. The brigade had been mobilised at the beginning when the conflict broke out when it went to Titova Korenica and was transferred to Jasenovac. In other words, it never disbanded and no need for repeated mobilisation; there was always one part of the brigade in existence. However, battalions were being mobilised in order to implement certain tasks. During such mobilisation process of the battalion, it becomes part of the brigade and it's under my competence. Once the task is finished, it is disbanded and the soldiers are being sent home, becoming civilians. In other words, the brigade no longer held any sway over them while they were in their homes. Until they are recalled, the brigade could not take any measures against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the brigade command, how many people were there in Lusci Palanka?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: For the most part, the brigade command had 50 per cent of officers present, while the other half were at home, and then they rotated. The ones who were in the brigade would go home and the ones who were at home came to the brigade. The same principle was applied to battalion commands. As for the other units, they were engaged as I have already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How are simple soldiers gathered? In other words, then, and how long do they remain implementing their tasks as well as when their tasks are finished, what is done with them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: At the beginning, say in May or April when we arrived, they were mostly engaged for a single day when we wanted to put villages under control to disarm them. Then they would be engaged by the day, and when their tasks were completed, they were released to go home. Later on, however, the corps command made use of those battalions at certain fronts and then they would go there for ten days, following which they were replaced by another unit and they returned home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any conditions in place to billet greater numbers of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: There were no such conditions for the billeting of soldiers other than those who were with the command. They were mostly billeted in the houses nearby. In other words, I had no conditions in place to be able to organise any kind of detention or prison. If any brigade member was brought in, they were placed in a civilian prison which was in the MUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are nearing the end. I wanted to announce this for the sake of the Prosecution so that they know that I would be requiring less time than I initially asked for. Let us go back to the Crisis Staff. Were Crisis Staff decisions forwarded to your brigade and its command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The decisions of the Crisis Staff were not forwarded whatsoever. Those that I did manage to see as part of the indictment submitted against me, I see that they frequently occurred without any signature and it never says that they were forwarded to the brigade command. They should cite distribution, but none of that exists. I think they never even tried to forward them because they knew I wouldn't act upon them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, thank you for responding to our questions. At this point in time, I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Jeremy, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And good morning, Mr. Basara.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to start by clarifying your previous interviews with the Office of the Prosecutor and your previous prior testimony before this Tribunal. So, first of all, you have mentioned it today but you testified in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case on 12th and 13th of October 2009; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you told the truth during that testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: As far as I know, I told the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were also interviewed as a suspect by the OTP on the 31st of August, 2002; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you also told the truth during that interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And lastly you were interviewed as a suspect again by the OTP on the 31st of March, 2009; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, again, you told the truth during that interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on now and discuss the arrival of the 6th Brigade in Sanski Most. Now, this was on the 3rd of April, 1992; correct.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the -- you brought the brigade to Sanski Most pursuant to an order from General Talic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber has received evidence - that's P3837 - that the Serb Assembly of Sanski Most declared the municipality part of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on this same day, the 3rd of April, 1992. You were aware that the arrival of your brigade coincided with this declaration. Yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just -- it seems your answer came before --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware. I wasn't aware of that because I was not in contact at all with the municipal organs. It was based on my orders that I brought the brigade in with the task of preparing conflict in the territory of the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when your -- when your brigade arrived in Sanski Most, the 6th Brigade, in terms of the numbers of men that you had within this brigade during 1992, I understand that the numbers reached up to around 4.000 men in July and August 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: While the brigade was in Jasenovac it had perhaps 1.000 men at the most. Very few Muslims and Croats responded to the brigade calls. Thus it was manned through one battalion from Bosanski Novi, which was later renamed into Novi Grad and there was a company from Kljuc as part of the brigade. When the brigade arrived in Sanski Most, I returned the Novi Grad Battalion as well as the Kljuc Company to their original locations. I manned the rest of the units as best I could so that the brigade could have a greater number of fighters so that I could implement this task of preventing conflicts in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when you say you manned the brigade as best you could, I'll remind that you in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case you said that the numbers in the brigade were three and a half thousand to 4.000 in July and August of 1992. Is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: That was in August. I just explained to you the situation in April, when it arrived, as well as in May. In August, however, I do know that it was the number. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you mentioned that you didn't have a relationship with the -- you didn't have contact with the municipal organs on your arrival into Sanski Most but it's correct, is it not, that the order that General Talic issued to you pursuant to which you brought the 6th Brigade to Sanski Most asked you to begin to co-ordinate with the organs of government in Sanski Most. That's correct; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, co-ordination had to do with the manning of the brigade in terms of co-operating with the Secretariat of National Defence. As regards any political activities, the brigade was under no obligation to engage in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's exactly take a quick like at P2865, please, and this is an order from the 5th Corps to the 6th Partisan Brigade and dated 1st of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the 6th Partisan brigade the same thing as the 6th Krajina Brigade or the Sana Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: My understanding is that it is and perhaps the witness can confirm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Basara, very quickly, I think the document is on the screen before us now. We see the document is dated the 1st of April, 1992. And we see if we go to the -- page 3 of the English and page 2 of the -- and page 3 of the B/C/S, we see that it's signed by Commander Major-General Momir Talic. And if we can go back to -- Colonel Basara, you see Major-General Talic's signature there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we can go back to -- the first page of this document, please. I want to focus your attention on the paragraph that is two above point number 2, which reads: "Establish full co-operation with the organs of government in Sanski Most municipality and collaboration with the TO and police units." So, Colonel Basara, does that refresh your recollection that that was what was required of you on arriving into Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: We can see that in the order. However, that co-operation included security organs and the police in terms of gathering information and reports from the field. As regards the TO, I did establish co-operation with its commander, Nijaz Halilovic, for the most part. As regards municipal organs, it involved the manning of units rather than any other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to the nature of the co-operation between your brigade and the organs of government in Sanski Most. However, you'll agree with me that there is no reference here of restricting that co-operation simply to the manning of units rather than other tasks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: You see, this is just a formulation when certain tasks are being issued by a command. However, in the field, things look different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And as I say, we'll get to how things looked in the field. Let's move on. Now, you left your position as commander of the 6th Brigade in middle of December 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Upon my request, I wanted to leave the position of commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And following a brief period of time in Belgrade, you were then appointed commander of an operations group in Prijedor between March and August 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in August 1993, you retired for the last time from the VRS and you went to Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I did not retire. I had already retired as officer. I simply left the corps and the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And from that point onwards, you no longer had a position in the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Correct. I had no position. I was a simple retiree, living in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So it's correct that after you retired on -- sorry, after you left the VRS in August 1993, you went to Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: That is where my family was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did you return to Sanski Most before the end of the war in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I think I did twice to see my wife's parents who were over 80 years old. I would stay for a couple of days perhaps. In terms of any kind of participation in the brigade, there was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like to move on now and in the moments that we have -- the few minutes we have before we'll break, I'd like to discuss your relationship with General Talic, your corps commander. Now, you knew General Talic well; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I knew him well because I used to teach at the Military Academy. I know him since his time as a cadet. He knew me and treated me with respect during the period of my engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in your 2002 interview with the OTP, you described General Talic as a very active commander in the sense that he wanted to know what was going on as far as knowledge of events was concerned. That's -- that's correct; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you also said that in your view he was not an active commander in the sense of actually commanding operations themselves and you said in comparison with -- with, for example, General Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: It is correct that I said that he was not active in directing activities in terms of his participation. He was more the sort of commander who commanded from his command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when you compared that style of command to the more active style of command of General Mladic, were you basing this on any personal observations that you had of General Mladic's active command style?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I did not know General Mladic at all. I had no occasion to meet him, but based on what I could follow, I concluded that General Mladic was an officer who wanted to know everything, follow everything, and participate in things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that conclusion was based on General Mladic's reputation within the VRS. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we're at the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Basara, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after that. We'll resume at ten minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we establish that the videolink is still working well?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, we can hear and see you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, we left off talking about -- on the topic of General Talic. I'd now like to move to the related topic of reports that your brigade would send to General Talic in the corps command. And this is something that you previously discussed. Now, your brigade sent regular daily reports to the corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, I did not sign all of them, so I don't know whether they went every day. At any rate, this was sent through the duty officer. That is to say the duty officer of the brigade command was the one to compile that report, so I don't know whether these reports were sent every day. Most often the duty officer would sign these reports and send them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And would you say then that General Talic -- or you would say and you previously said this, that General Talic was well-informed about events that were occurring in the area of the 6th Brigade in Sanski Most; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, he received most of his information through personal conversations with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But I'm correct when I say that when reports were sent from the command post in your brigade, then your experience and experience that you've previously discussed is that there was always someone at the corps command to receive those daily reports; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, certainly duty service was organised and the duty officer at the corps received these reports. Now, to what extent was General Talic interested in reading and following all these reports, that is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when you say that General Talic received information through personal conversations with you, those conversations were frequent; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, I didn't talk to him often but every time we met, I would familiarize him with the situation in the territory and everything we did and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, maybe we'll return to this in a little more detail later. Now, I'd like to move to the topic of military police. During 1992, your brigade had first a platoon and later a company of military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And there were approximately 90 men in this company of military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly how many there were, but it could have been over 80, over 80 men, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. Witness, isn't it true that in the control and command structure reporting is very important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, I wondered when you said, well, what -- he got his information by incidental conversations with you, if you would see him you would tell him something. That sounds very unmilitary. Could you explain why a structured --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you just said. Witness, could you repeat what you said because the interpreters couldn't catch your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we started speaking at the same time, so then I stopped. I wished to say that the superior command received information mostly through the reports from the duty service. That is to say, everything that happened during the course of the day was supposed to be reported on. However, often it depended on the duty officer involved, the one who was supposed to write that report. So the command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that this information that was necessary was information that General Talic received from personal conversations with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- that's still not entirely clear to me. You say, on the one hand, it was the duty officer who did the reporting and that the necessary information General Talic received in personal conversations with you. Could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, necessary information, I'm saying the information that he could not receive through reports of the duty service. That is to say, the duty officers. Since I knew more than the duty officer, then he could receive such information from me. Furthermore, officers, according to their own lines of work, would provide information. For example, for morale and training, such an officer was -- would report to his superior. Then the chief of engineering, the chief of security, also sent certain information to the security organs of the corps. So, in that way, the system of information was organised. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last portion of your answer was not understood by the interpreters. Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the organs at the brigade command, the organ for morale and training, this person would sometimes send reports when necessary to his organ at the corps command. Then the chief of engineering would send a report to the chief of engineering in the command. The security organ would send some information to the security organ in the corps. So there was that chain of command too. Then the duty officer's reports and then through personal contacts with me and all of that is how the corps commander received all his information and was supposed to be made aware of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us an example of what kind of information was conveyed to General Talic in personal conversations which could not be, as you said, could not be given to him in the normal reporting structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for information, and that is the overall situation in the territory where I often went and I worked in order to prevent a conflict and things like that, as far as disarmament was concerned and so on, the duty officer was not aware of all of this, and he could not provide information about that and the organs couldn't either. So when we meet up he would often ask me about certain information, he would express his interest and then I would provide that information to him, what I thought he had not received through the other organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Than happened just, if you happened to meet without any plan or any structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, it didn't just happen accidentally. He would ask me to come to the corps command. He would invite me. It didn't just happen that way. It was done when necessary. And when I would ask for something for the brigade, we would meet up. So we met up pretty often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just to follow up on these personal conversations, Mr. Basara, that you were having with General Talic. You previously indicated in reference to the crimes in Sanski Most that you were aware of, some of which you discuss in your statement, you've indicated that the crimes that you were aware of General Talic was also aware of. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, I think he did know. I cannot assert whether he did know or not but I know that he was being informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you know that he was being informed because your reporting on these crimes were included in your personal conversations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that for you, when that was I talked to him but I know that on the basis of all these reports, he believed that I, in relation to all other commanders in the territory, was the one who had carried out all the activities concerned in the most normal and regular way so in his understanding, there weren't many problems, crime, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, I'm not focussing on your own conduct right now. What I'm asking you about is the crimes that you say that you knew of, you say General Talic also knew about those crimes and I'm asking you how he knew about them and I think your answer is: He did know about them but you're not sure how. You're not sure whether they were conveyed in reports or in personal conversation, but he was nevertheless aware of the crimes in Sanski Most that you were aware of. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you are asked to switch off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main line was the duty officers -- well, whether he registered these crimes and whether he found out about them totally, that is something I cannot say. But information was sent through the duty officers' reports and other reports but I cannot remember now - it's been a very long time - I cannot remember whether in one of the conversation I said something to him about any one of these crimes. I cannot say that for sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But you previously indicated that you knew that General Talic was aware of crimes that were aware of, but you're now simply saying but your not sure how he became aware of those crimes. Is that -- do I understand your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
