utterances.text: I am telling you that he was supposed to find out about that through the duty service reports and it depends whether they reported to him about that, and I thought that he knew about it because he was supposed to have received these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So if the -- if the reports on the crimes were not included in the duty officer reports, then he obviously found out some other way; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know any other way. I mean, I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. You were previously asked in the 2002 interview whether the crimes that were aware of, whether General Talic was also aware of those crimes. And you indicated that the crimes that you knew were committed General Talic was also aware of. So what was the basis for that observation, for that comment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, I believed because of the reports on the system on the basis of which we worked I believe that he knew about all of that. I did not double-check. I did not ask him whether he knew about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So you're saying it -- it was an assumption that you -- that you made; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes, the assumption is that he knew, just like I found out about many things although I did not receive reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we'll get to the detail of these crimes. But the crimes that were aware of it was your obligation to report those to your superior officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I told you that I personally didn't have to do that. So there's the command, everybody had their own duties. There was the security organ that reported in great detail to their superior in the corps command. So all of that, all this information, had to arrive in the corps command. I could not manage everything as the commander. In addition to all of my duties and obligations, I could not think of each and every detail. I could not worry about whether someone had found out about everything or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I would like to ask for one clarification. Mr. Basara, you said you could not manage everything as the commander. But as the commander, did you have a responsibility for a proper reporting system by your duty officers and by the assistant commanders of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what we did. That is to say, all the organs of command reported along their own lines and chains, and the duty officer did that too. At first, I was the only professional soldier in my brigade. I had so many obligations. I had such a lot of work that I could not follow all of this in great detail and I could not stand behind every report, read and sign each and every report, because I had to feed the troops, provide them with clothing, ammunition, everything else, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, I would like to stop you here. I'm not talking about feeding the troops or everything else. Was it your responsibility as a superior -- as the commander of the brigade, to supervise your subordinates, including the desk officer and the duty officer, that they fulfilled their obligations properly, according to the rules and the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did that. That's my duty as commander and I'm not denying that. I did that to the best of my ability, as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And following up on Judge Fluegge's question, you've previously indicated that while you were not aware of the content of every daily report, the reports did, nevertheless, go to the corps command every day. And that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I cannot claim anything because I did not have insight, and I was not always at the corps command, and I cannot claim that every day they went so I cannot assert that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you the following: On a regular basis, were daily reports sent? I'm not asking whether you may have missed one or two, but was it a routine that daily reports were sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a routine to have daily reports sent that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, let's -- Colonel Basara, let's move to a different topic which you discuss in your statement and that is the relationship that you cultivated with the Muslims and Croats in Sanski Most. Now, in paragraph 9 of your statement, your position seems to be broadly that you endeavoured to prevent conflicts between the ethnic groups in Sanski Most and that you had talks with representatives of the Muslims and the Croats and the Serbs in Sanski Most and you did what you referred to as trying to defuse the heated situation. That's correct; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: It is correct. Together with Nijaz Halilovic, I visited all the villages, all the Muslim villages in the broader area of the road from Sanski Most to Lusci Palanka in the villages or in the parts of town -- the town of Sanski Most, I'm not sure where we were, actually. It's been a very long time. However, on the basis of the conclusion and opinion of Nijaz Halilovic, we visited these villages. We assembled people, talked to them, asked them not to have any conflicts taking place so that no one would use weapons, especially not against members of the brigade. This would lead to revenge from the Serb people and I tried to explain that we should go on living in that territory as we had been living until then, living a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: -- on a higher level, like the leadership of the Muslims in Sarajevo when the JNA was attacked and when they started conflicts, then these plans of mine and all of that was simply buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, at the same time that you were going from village to village holding these discussions with Muslims and Croats in Sanski Most, you were also organising and arming Serbs in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I did not organise this and I did not arm them. Most Serbs were already armed by then. I had nowhere to get these weapons. Most of them were armed already. Most Serbs already had weapons at that time, and I just made an effort to bring them all under a command, to involve them in certain units so that I could exercise more control over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's take a look at a document in connection with your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P2365. And, Your Honours, this is the document I mentioned as part of the preliminary that we have the revised translation for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you had an opportunity to look at the new translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did not from the opportunity to check the whole translation, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. No, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although I left it with my Case Manager. It should be done over this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We've provided a short document highlighting the changes between the two versions so I hope that will be a quick process.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Basara, you recognised the document on the screen before you; yes? It's written in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes, it's my handwriting. And these people from the brigade, I mean, some officers, they had the intention of writing the history of the brigade and they asked me to write something is and I wrote something sort of shorter, and I gave them this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. So you previously said that you wrote this at the end of 1992 or early 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't know when exactly I wrote it. I just know that they asked me to do it and that I did. It was such a long time ago that I no longer remember when I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I understand that. Do you recall whether you wrote it after you were no longer commander of the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I think -- I don't know. I don't know if I wrote it when I was no longer commander of the 6th Brigade. It could also be just before my departure or when I commanded the operational group, but I can't say that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at the contents of this document, and I'd like to go please to page 2 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S. And directing your attention to number 4, towards the top of the page, we read that: "Interethnic conflicts intensified in the municipalities of Sanski Most, Prijedor and Kljuc in March 1991." Now I'm correct in saying that that should be March 1992; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No. It refers to the period before my arrival in the brigade. I received reports from my relatives in Lusci Palanka about the situation in that part of the territory and this is what it pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Then in the next paragraph when we see the reference to the 1st Krajina Corps withdrawing the 6th from Jasenovac and Sanski Most, and we see the reference to 3rd of April 1991, the 6th being transferred to Sanski Most, that -- at least that paragraph should be a reference to the 3rd of April 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes. That the brigade arrived from Jasenovac to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: On the 3rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, this is not the next paragraph, but the next sentence just to make it clear for the record. You said in the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in the next -- in the next sentence down, we read as follows, Colonel Basara: "After the brigade came to this area, the Muslims and Croats became afraid while the Serbs heaved a sigh of relief. However, the brigade was not fully replenished and since the 1st Battalion was almost entirely from Novi Grad, they requested to go to their own area. We had to arm the Serbs quickly and quickly replenish our units. Since we, as JNA units, were tasked with preventing interethnic conflicts, i.e., the slaughter of the Serbian people, we could not be seen to be arming the Serbs in public. We worked along two lines: The first was to organise and arm the Serbian people; and the second to negotiate and convince the Muslims and Croats to remain loyal and live together with the Serbs. The negotiations were about the division of power. We had to resort to trickery to make it possible for us to arm Serbs publicly and legally." Colonel Basara, my question is this: According to your own words, while you were negotiating with the non-Serbs in Sanski Most, you were also organising and arming the Serbs, the Serbs in Sanski Most. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Listen, if I may, I'd like to give a more extensive explanation and then you will understand why I wrote it the way I did, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, I'd ask you to be as focussed as you can be in any short explanation that you provide.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: As regards the explanation, it is as follows. At a session of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly where all three peoples were represented, I proposed the following, wishing to stay true to what I was trying to explain the Muslims in those villages. I wanted to ask them to establish a brigade reflecting the ethnic makeup in the territory which was 50 per cent Serbs and 50 Muslims and Croats --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, I'm sorry to interrupt you. This, I think is dealt with in your statement and I'll also deal with this in my next question, so once I've asked that question and you've provided your answer, then you'll have another opportunity to provide any additional answer, if you think that that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: What I said, that we were arming them, it has to do with the following. I am an ethnic Serb, and I was being accused by Serbs of assisting Muslims and acting as a pro-Muslim element, that I married a Muslim woman and was helping the Muslims. That is why in this text I wrote, I had to wiggle my way out of being accused as a traitor of the Serb people who worked solely for the benefit of Muslims. I had to explain one thing to one side and another thing to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, let's stick to the facts. Did you arm Serbs or not? Apart from what reasons you had. Or were you involved in arming Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in no position to arm them because I had no arms. As I said, the Serbs, most of them had already had weapons, and I only placed them in units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslims did not wish to respond and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in your own handwriting, we read that you had to arm the Serbs quickly and quickly replenish your orders. You did not write, We didn't have to arm the Serbs because they had weapons already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't write it. You now insist on that, but I couldn't put it in those words. I couldn't say they had weapons. This formulation needn't necessarily have been true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you saying that what you wrote down is not what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It isn't as it happened because most of them had already had weapons. However, I don't see any crime in arming one's own people, when the other side, Muslims and Croats, were also arming themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer, that there was nothing wrong in arming them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If one side is arming themselves, the Muslims, and if they are attacking the units of the JNA, then normally the Serbs had the right to arm themselves as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you thought that it was justified to arm them for this reason and that's why it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said I wrote it this way because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I didn't ask you why you wrote it the way you did. I asked you a question whether the fact that the other ethnic groups had armed themselves was, for you, the justification to be involved in arming the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believed that the Serbs, too, had the right to do that if the Muslims were arming themselves and initiating aggression. I thought, under those circumstances, the Serbs were entitled to arms as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was, for you, the reason to be involved in arming the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not go to collect any weapons and I did not distribute them. I simply ordered that those people be included in the units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- people gained possession of weapons in many, many different ways. I don't even know which ways exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not the language you used in your own handwriting, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said so already why I wrote it the way I did. There was already a witch hunt against me saying that as the commander, I was a pro-Muslim element so I had to put a stop to such rumours so that I wouldn't be recorded in history as ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, but then what you say, I wrote it just to re-write history and to avoid being blamed, but it didn't happen as I wrote it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that it didn't. It didn't happen as I wrote it because I wrote it this way with a particular goal in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you're telling us that you're giving us the reason why you wrote it. And, at the same time, you give us a justification for arming Serbs. If it didn't happen, why would be bother about whether it would be justified or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't deal with that much. My understanding was simply that if one side was being armed, the other side was entitled to it as well. I did not give any such right to anyone. That was my understanding. That was the general understanding in existence at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're telling us now is that although it would have been justified to arm the Serbs and although you did write down that Serbs were armed, that it, nevertheless, did not happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying they were not being armed at all. I'm just saying that most of them had already had weapons. If somebody received weapons at that time, there were far fewer of them than there were of those who already had weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you said Serbs were armed but the quantity was relatively low?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who were armed later on, their numbers were smaller compared to the ones who already had weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Colonel Basara, you actually were also involved in arming of Serbs in Sanski Most in 1991. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber has received evidence that Serbs were being armed in Sanski Most in 1991 and that they were being organised and armed by a man called Rajko Stojanovic. And that's P2362. You knew Rajko Stojanovic, didn't you, Colonel Basara?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I met Rajko Stojanovic later on when I arrived in the area of Sanski Most. In his house on the ground floor, he had a cafe and that is where weapons were being deposited, the same weapons that had been taken from the Sanski Most warehouse. Somebody probably made this connection, saying that he was arming people. However, I am not aware of that fact. I only know, as I said already, that the TO weapons when they were pulled out of Sanski Most were stored with him to a great extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say, "I met Rajko Stojanovic later on when I arrived in the area of Sanski Most," was that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: In April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. So your evidence is that you didn't know this man before that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Correct. I don't know if I met him anywhere but we were officially introduced in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when you say in your previous answers that someone probably made this connection saying that Rajko Stojanovic was arming people, that's actually a connection that you make in your handwritten history in the document before us. Could we take a look at the first page of this please, page 1, I'd like to focus on paragraph 2. There, Colonel Basara, we read: "I was in Lusci Palanka in late September and early October 1991. The reason I went there was to help the Serbian people organise for defence against the attack of Muslims and Croats. Rajko Stojanovic knows the most about it so he can say more about it if necessary, because I do not have much time." So, Colonel Basara, in fact, you met Rajko Stojanovic not in 1992 but in 1991 and you were then aware of this arming during this period; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Given the fact that I wrote this subsequently, it is probable that this does not tally. I don't recall having met him in 1991. We may have met each other somewhere along the way, but I can't state that it is actually true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, your information about this man seems to be rather specific. You don't say that you simply met him in passing on the road. You actually talk about what he was actually involved in, and you suggested you have more information than you're able to include in this war history. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say that later on I did not learn of this Rajko. He later on became company commander in one of the battalions. Hence, I met Rajko later on. Probably we conversed and later on, as I was writing this, I made that link.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So if I understand your position correctly, you were in Lusci Palanka in late September, October 1991 you were there to help the Serbian people organise for their defence against the Muslims and Croats. At that point, you weren't aware of Rajko Stojanovic but you subsequently became aware of it and in writing this history, you retrospectively say he'll also know a bit about that, a bit about what I was doing in September and October 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Probably that is the source it comes from.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are losing the witness. We can't hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke to some of the neighbours, and then I told them how to position themselves in order not to have 1941 repeated, that the Serbs would not be exterminated from the senior.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm not talking about 1941. I'm focussing on what you were doing in September and early October 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, in all fairness to the witness, that is what he -- what was the -- the -- the core of his answer. He -- he spoke to some of the neighbours and told them how to position themselves in order not to have a repetition of 1941. So he focussed his answer primarily what did he in 1991, although a reference was made as part of his activities that he referred -- that he did it for the purposes of a non-repetition of what happened in 1941. So I think it's not fair to the witness that he was not asked about 1941. He focussed his answer relatively well to your question. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. And we can see that the translators could not hear actually the beginning of the answer of this witness and he was explaining his whereabouts at that time and how much time he spent in Lusci Palanka. So I think [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... could we invite the witness -- Witness, not all of your answer was caught by the interpreters. Could you tell us what you said just before you told us that you spoke to some of the neighbours. What did you tell us before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, I said that in that period, I did not spend any significant amounts of time in the area. I only came to visit my wife's parents. I spent only a few days there, talking to the neighbours. They were very afraid of seeing 1941 repeated because the Muslims were better armed and still arming. I talked to them about it and went back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Rajko Stojanovic could tell us more about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Because in the text which is before us, after you said that the reason was to help the Serbian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the first part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the first part of your answer. And I think it's better to wait until I've finished my question usually before you start your answer because then your words are easily lost. Could you repeat the beginning of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I did not spend any significant time in the area of Lusci Palanka at the time. I was there for only two to three days, visiting my wife's parents and my relatives. At the time, I talked to the neighbours I met. They were very afraid. They were afraid of seeing 1941 happen again. They were telling me how the Muslims were arming themselves. We talked about it, and I suggested some ways for them to organise themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. -- it's not what you write down that you went there to see your family and then in the margin of that spoke to some neighbours. What you have written down is that you -- the reason why you went there is to help the Serbian people organise the defence. It being the reason why you went there. But I leave it to that at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You hold on tight to my words, but I'm telling you what is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We'll shortly move away from this document, Colonel Basara, but I'd like to hold on tight to some other words that you include here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2 of the English, please, and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now referring first to your statement in paragraph 17 and 18, you refer to -- you state that before the split of the MUP and the division of power in Sanski Most you propose that Muslims and Croats should be -- should assist you in establishing a brigade that would be comprised of 50 per cent Serb population and 50 per cent Muslim and Croat population. And in the next paragraph, you talk about how the president of the Executive Board of the Sanski Most municipality Mirzet Karabeg asked you if battalions of the mixed brigade would go to Kupres to fight and you say that you told him that you had two battalions in the brigade that were mostly comprised of Serbs and that these battalions would go to Kupres if need be. Now, with those two paragraphs in mind I'd like to refer you back to paragraph 4 of this handwritten history and I'd like to take to you where I left off reading when we last looked at this paragraph and we read halfway through paragraph 4: "A story was invented that the commander of the 1 KK ordered that the 6th be promoted from a light to an infantry brigade so that it could have up to 15 battalions and could be additionally mobilised as soon as possible to prevent Muslims" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I think we need to go to the next page in the B/C/S. "To prevent Muslims and Croats from joining the brigade it was said that the brigade would be going to Kupres as soon as mobilisation was completed?"

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara, in fact, you did the exact opposite to what you say you did in the statement. You told the Muslims and the Croats that the brigade would be going to Kupres for the express purpose of ensuring that they did not enlist. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not correct. And I cannot see it here now. But I doubt that. I doubt that that's what I wrote. Because my intention was to establish such a brigade and to secure the territory of the municipality of Sanski Most in a circular fashion and had the Muslims and Croats responded, that's exactly what I would have done. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. You started by doubting whether that's what you wrote, and Mr. Jeremy will now take you to the passage and to see whether you did write what he said or not. Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So if we can look at page 3 and we're looking at halfway down -- page 3 in the B/C/S, please, halfway down, paragraph 4, and Colonel Basara, can you see the sentence that begins with: "A story was invented ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is almost at the bottom of the page, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It should be one, two, three, four, five, six -- six or seven lines or so up from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I got the impression in B/C/S it is four lines from the bottom where command of the 1st Krajina Corps is specifically referred to. Could you reed that, Mr. Basara? Have you found --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st commander of the 1st Krajina Corps ordered that the 6th be re-established from a light brigade to an infantry brigade. And that it could have 15 battalions and the brigade would have to be additionally mobilised as soon as possible. I've just read that and that is what I wrote and that is what happened. Namely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- witness I'll stop you. Could you please continue to read. We'll change the page, and you start with "da Muslimani." Could you read that portion as well? The last two words being, "da Muslimani," and we move now to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the brigade after the mobilisation is over should go to Kupres and then conditions were created for a legal mobilisation. That's what's written there. However, my idea was that the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. We're just still establishing what you wrote. Mr. -- I think we started with the commander of the 1st Krajina Brigade and then there's a portion in English --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, could you please assist. You have the -- Mr. Jeremy is focussing specifically on the lines that to prevent Muslims and Croats from joining the brigade. From what I hear from the witness, he doesn't -- he has not read that, which either it isn't there or he left it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I didn't -- didn't hear that particular part either, Your Honours, I wonder if we could ask the witness to again slowly read that final sentence just to see if it's an oversight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we move to the previous page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you read -- Witness, could you read -- first of all, do you find a line where it says: "A story was invented that the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps ordered that the 6th be promoted from a light to an infantry brigade ..." Do you see that line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you read the text from -- starting with that sentence. And continue to read -- and continue to read until I ask you to stop.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A story was invented that the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps had ordered that the 6th be renamed from a light into an infantry brigade and that it could have even up to 15 battalions and that the brigade would have to be additionally mobilised as soon as possible. In order not to have Muslims and Croats come to the brigade, it was said that the brigade as soon as mobilisation would be completed should go to Kupres. Then conditions were created to legally" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- that's sufficient for the time being, Mr. Jeremy, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Witness, we did this -- witness, would you please wait for a second. Witness, would you -- Witness, would you wait for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not for you to put questions. You earlier doubted whether the portion you now just read, whether you had written that. I think we have established now that you did write the text as you just read it to us. Mr. Jeremy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, contrary to what you say in your statements, the truth is that you took steps, steps that we've looked at here, to actively discourage Muslims and Croats from enlisting in the 6th Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: That is not correct. Because, in this sentence, where it says "it was said," it's not that I said that they would go to Kupres. Rather, these were news that were being spread by the Serbs who attended the session of the assembly when I suggested that such a brigade be formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So in your war time record of the 6th Brigade you're simply recounting what others said rather than what you yourself said. Is that -- that's your position on this paragraph or on this document or on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: What is written in this paragraph, well, I already explained that to you why I wrote it that way. Because I could not allow people to think that I was against arming the Serbs and that I'm arming Muslims and Croats with the proposal that I had made and that I wished to man the brigade in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And just before we reach our break time, you seem to be suggesting that you would write some things in this document to appease somebody in the municipality. And who -- who was it that you were trying to appease?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I did not have the intention to relent in any way. I just didn't want any slander. I didn't want them to say that I was pro-Muslim and that I was a traitor of the Serb people. That's why I wrote it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when you're referring --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: After --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: When you're referring -- sir, when you're referring to "them," do I understand you to be referring to the Serbian political authorities in Sanski Most or are you referring to the -- to the military authorities in Sanski Most? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: The political authorities. Because immediately at that meeting Rasula said to me, Colonel, yet again, you want to create brotherhood and unity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when you wrote this, you were a colonel in the VRS in charge of many thousands of soldiers, but you felt you needed to write this to appease Rasula; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Not only Rasula but also around the brigade. People were spreading this like news, that in battalions they were taking in all the Muslims and Croats who would report there. And then from the political leadership from the Serbs that is to say, Rasula, Vrkes and I don't know what was being bandied about was I was a pro-Muslim element they went to see Talic asking him to dismiss me and so on. Do understand the conditions under which I was working?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I have two very short questions of fact for you. Was it said that the brigade would be going to Kupres as soon as mobilisation was completed? Was that said or was that not said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that. I did not convey that because I did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... witness, I didn't ask you whether you said that. My question was whether it was said that the brigade would be going to Kupres --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably it was said. Since I heard people saying in Sanski Most that the brigade, once it is formed, it is going against Kupres, and I was saying to the Muslim leadership that the brigade would not go there but rather it would go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, please stick to my questions. So you said most probably that was said. Was that said to prevent Muslims and Croats from joining the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably somebody who was trying to spread such a rumour, and misinformation spreads quickly most often. Such people tried to achieve that. Rather, they didn't want to have Muslims and Croats join the brigade. However, I did not do that because I suggested that that kind of brigade be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not writing about rumours but you presented for a fact that it was said, "to prevent Muslims and Croats from joining the brigade." Do I understand that that's not what you know happened or that it was just rumours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were rumours that were heard on the ground. Now whether they came from Serbs or Muslims or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you, Witness, you have answered my question. We'll take a break. We'll resume at a quarter to 2.00. We take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we check whether the videolink is functioning well?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, we can see -- see and hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same is true from this side. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, during your discussions -- your questions from Mr. Lukic this morning, you indicated that General Talic did not come to Sanski Most during the time that you were commander of the 6th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And during your testimony this morning, you also mentioned that you were present at a meeting of various representatives of the ethnic groups in Sanski Most at the municipal assembly building. Now, this meeting was on the 20th of May, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I often attended -- I mean, I don't know which assembly meeting you mean. Whenever they invited me and when I knew about the session, then I would always attend sessions that were attended by Muslim, Croat and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And when you attended at least one of those sessions, do you recall that General Talic was actually present there with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: No, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take a look at a document in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P3294, and that's the diary of Nedjeljko Rasula. We've discussed Rasula this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You knew who he was, Mr. Basara; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And he was the president of the municipality of Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we please go to page 22 in the English, please, and 20 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just at the bottom, in the English, we see "meeting 20th of April 1992." And if we could go to the next page in the English, please. Now, Colonel Basara, focussing your attention on the left side of the page in the original language, we see the date the 20th of April, 1992, and we see a list of those persons present at this particular meeting. Do you see General Talic's name listed there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Well, it's written there, General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you see your own name listed there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: General Talic ... Colonel Basara.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And seeing your own name there together with General Talic's name, does that refresh your recollection that General Talic did, in fact, visit the municipality of Sanski Most and also attend at least one meeting in the municipality building with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't remember any of that. I tried to remember because I read certain things, but I simply could not remember. It would be natural if he was in Sanski Most for him to come to the brigade command as well. But, again, as I've said, I don't remember that at all. I remember this one meeting that was attended by Lieutenant-Colonel Talic, his first name is Mustafa or something like that. And somehow I seem to think that they've confused him with General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, earlier, page 75, you referred to the 20th of May, whereas now, was that a slip of the tongue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That was a slip of the tongue. Thank you for correcting me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is hereby then corrected. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, Colonel Basara, just to understand your last answer, is it your understanding that this -- this record of the -- of this meeting is incorrect in so far as it refers to General Talic and you think it should be referring to a different Talic. Is that your recollection of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't recall that meeting at all, and I cannot remember General Talic being there at all. As for this other one, I eventually did remember him, but I don't remember about General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you were actually asked about this meeting during your testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, and you indicated that General Talic was present at this meeting because it was part of his work as commander to inspect units and to maintain contact with the leadership of Sanski Most. Would you provide that same answer today?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't remember that at all. That statement of mine. That testimony of mine. That I claimed anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's take a quick look at that. Just -- it might refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 31875. That's Colonel Basara's testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case. If we could please go to page 24. And, sorry, if we could go back one page just to establish the meeting, it's the same meeting we're now talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So we see at -- and Colonel Basara, there isn't a translation of this document for you so I'd ask you to listen closely to my words. We see at line 15 that the questioning lawyer is asking you to look at a record of a meeting that was apparently held on the 20th of April with yourself and General Talic and members of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you were asked about members present. You -- you actually indicated that whereas there's a reference to a Major Zekaj, it should be a reference to Zeljaja. Now it says representatives of the SDS, SDA and HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could just scroll up a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, "Was this the only meeting before the take-over that took place where General Talic attended?" Your answer was as follows: "I think it was the only one attended by General Talic but I can hardly remember what was discussed and how the meeting ran. "Q. I'm just going to ask you about two matters. But that was only one attended by General Talic, can you remember why General Talic had come to Sanski Most that day? "A. Well, it was part of his work as commander to inspect units and to maintain contact with the leadership of the municipality in Sanski Most." My question to you now, Colonel Basara, is: Having listened to me reading your testimony in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case does that refresh your recollection about this meeting and your knowledge about General Talic's presence at this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I hope you can believe me that I don't remember anything from that meeting. I even gave this some thought and I cannot link all of that up, that he was at this meeting, that I was at that meeting. So that meeting probably did not remain in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Would you agree with me that when you testified in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case six years ago, your memory would have been fresher?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I was six years younger, and it is likely that I could remember some things then that I couldn't remember now, so that would be my answer more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, do you also remember and I'm asking you to reach further back to 2002 but on the topic of the municipality building that -- that was attacked in -- on the 19th of April, 1992, you were asked about whether you considered that attack to be illegal, and you indicated that you did, indeed, consider the attack on the municipality building to be illegal. Would you give the same answer today?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't know. I'd like to see where it says that I said so. That it was an illegal attack. Speaking from this position today, I think it was the Serbs' right to regain possession of the municipal building. It had been agreed they remain in the municipal building and that the Muslims go to the premises of a company. The same goes for their MUP. Instead, they took over the municipal building. So perhaps there was some kind of misinterpretation on somebody's part, in terms of me saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have an opportunity to check that, Witness. If there's any doubt about it, then it will be done. Mr. Jeremy, the Chamber would appreciate if it would be verified whether that's really what the witness had said during that interview. That's one. Second, let's not spend too much time on it because it's not testimony of fact but, rather, opinion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And actually I will move on but I would like to tender the transcript page from the Stanisic and Zupljanin testimony that we just saw while the witness didn't dispute what was -- his answers, he didn't actually confirm them so I would like to tender this particular page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the number would be P7320.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. And about his interview, Mr. Jeremy, what would you like to do with that. You read it to him and, of course, in all fairness to the Defence and to the witness, it should be verified whether -- really, perhaps the parties could stipulate on whether that was said. May I take it has been audio recorded as at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, my understanding that there is an audio record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No video record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, I don't think there's a video record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite the parties to sit together and see whether they can verify whether the written text corresponds with the audio. Witness, it will be verified whether what was read to you as part of your statement, whether those were words you really uttered at the time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, I'd look to move on now to a different topic and that's the topic of the strategic objectives which you make mention of in your statement. Now, you say in paragraph 19 of your statement that you were not at the meeting which formulated the six strategic objectives for the Serb people on the 12th of May, 1992. You were instead at a meeting after the liberation of Jajce. Now, the meeting regarding the six strategic objectives that you refer to here is the -- the 16th Assembly Session that was held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't recall at all when it was held, and I don't know in which statement I referred to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It's all right, sir. Paragraph 19 of the statement that you've provided to this Chamber that you have sworn to the truth of today, you state as follows: "I was not at the meeting which formulated the six strategic objectives for the Serb people. On 12 May 1992, I was at a meeting after the liberation of Jajce." Just so you understand that's what prompted me to mention that you mentioned the six strategic objectives in your statement. Now, while you were not at that meeting, you were, nevertheless, at another meeting two days after the 16th Assembly Session, namely, on the 14th of May, where the strategic objectives were discussed. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Where did the assembly session take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The assembly session was discussed the strategic objectives was in Banja Luka on 12th of May. I understand that you have said that you weren't there, and I don't disputes that. What I'm asking you is: Were you present at a meeting in Kljuc on the 14th of May where you discussed, among other things, the six strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I came to Kljuc to attend a meeting, but when we started it, a battalion was being sent from Kljuc to a theatre of war and they were firing in the street. So much so that we couldn't keep working. Then the municipal assembly president, Mr. Banjac turned to General Galic who, at the time was colonel and commanded a division, asking him to go out and tell the people to stop shooting so that we could go on with our work? He didn't want to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Can I explain? And I went out to put a stop to that shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Therefore, I missed most of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that was a meeting you say that was attended by Banjac of -- president of the Kljuc municipality and also Colonel Galic. You do remember the meeting; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I do remember coming there and attending it at the beginning, but I had to leave to stop the battalion from shooting further because we could not conduct our work. I spoke to the soldiers and only returned at the end. I heard a couple of things, but other than that I had no idea that they were discussing any strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's take a look at that meeting and see if it refreshes your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P2867.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Colonel Basara we see there's stamp on right side, top right side of the document dated the 14th of May. We see that it's a meeting with presidents of municipalities in the zone of responsibility of the division. We see that the meeting lasted for two hours, 45 minutes, and we see the agenda. Agenda item 3 is: "Messages from the meeting on the armed services [sic] of Serbian Krajina and the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Banja Luka on the 12th of May 1992." And we see those attendees of the meeting, the first one is Colonel Galic, who you've mentioned already and the second one is yourself, Colonel Basara, and we see at number 5, there's a reference to a Jovo Banjac. So that's the same meeting that you've already mentioned; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: What I do remember is only what was discussed. As I said, it was a long time ago. I can't remember everything, but I do remember that I had to leave the meeting to stop the battalion from shooting and that I stayed outside for a while because the fighters were interested in many issues --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: So I spoke to them --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, you say you remember what was discussed and I'd like to show you a part of the minutes of the that meeting to see if you remember discussion of that particular part. Could we go to page 3 in this document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be an issue there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is an issue from the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the logic of the sentence the witness spoke - let me just - one second, please. The witness said, "What I do remember is what was discussed. As I said, it was a long time ago. I can't remember everything but I do remember that I had to leave." Now that may at least hint at a possible error. It's not very logic. Could you please seek verification of that answer before you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, sir, simply I'll ask you the question, the document indicates that there was a discussion of the strategic goals that were articulated at the municipal assembly meeting in Banja Luka on the 12th of May, 1992. My question is: Do you recall the discussion of those six strategic goals at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I don't. I have no recollection --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We couldn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you said after: I have no recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember at all what was discussed at the meeting. I can't make any connection between the strategic goals and the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, two very short questions. You were, however, aware of the six strategic goals; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Pardon? No, I don't recall the strategic goals at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: Although I may have mentioned them somewhere, but I don't remember anything in terms of content.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So is it your position that while you were brigade commander in Sanski Most, you were not aware of the six strategic goals? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I was not aware of it. At least to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And is it therefore also your position that these were not disseminated to units within your brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of their being forwarded to the units. It would have been very difficult to distribute it to the units which were not in one place. Many people were there their homes. If anyone was informed of anything, it could only have been partial and could take -- have taken place in battalion commands and brigade commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's leave it there for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we adjourn, I have one question, because it's not entirely clear to me, are you saying that today you have no recollection of the six strategic goals, or that you never had any knowledge of the six strategic goals and their contents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I can't remember right now, I can't tell you whether I knew anything about the strategic objectives at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, and I take it local time is the same as it is here, that is, at 9.30. But before you leave the videolink room, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have already given or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just before the witness leaves. I would kindly ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's too late, obviously. I wanted Mr. Ram to be notified that somebody should organise transportation for Mr. Basara tomorrow, at least, since we cannot see him. We organized his transportation this morning. My people from Belgrade, from my office cannot do it anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I take it telephone conversation with the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: VWS will also look into the matter. That's what Madam Registrar tells me. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that the videolink is still functioning so if there's anything about transportation which you would like to convey to the witness, Mr. Lukic, then we have an opportunity to do so right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would just like to inform Mr. Basara that Sasa Lukic is not able to transport him tomorrow to the same location, so we will try to find a solution through VWS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness -- everyone will work hard in order to make sure that you will be transported to the videolink location tomorrow morning. Then we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, the 21st of April, 9.30 in the morning, in this same Courtroom I, and we'll then continue the videolink. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of April, 2015, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
